Development of the RM 8.5 Instream Temperature Forecast Model

Source: vignettes/model-development-history.Rmd
model-development-history.Rmd

Abstract

This document records the development of a statistical model forecasting seven-day average daily maximum (7DADM) water temperature at Whychus Creek RM 8.5 at lead times of one to seven days, for use in Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) threshold management. Development proceeded from an inherited artificial neural network (ANN) approach, through a random forest (RF) model class selection, to the current formulation, in which the RF predicts the change in 7DADM from the value observed on the forecast issue date rather than the absolute temperature. The rationale for that formulation, and the evidence supporting it, are the primary subject of this document. The current model is treated as a working formulation rather than a final result; open questions are stated in Section 9.

1. Background and origin

The modelling approach was adapted from prior work by Spencer Sawaske (2023) on the Middle Fork John Day, retained in data-raw/scripts_from_spencer/. That work used an sklearn MLPRegressor over a compact predictor set:

X_M1 = [Q, Julian, Air_Max, Air_Min, Q_m1, Air_Max_m1, Air_Min_m1]

comprising discharge, day-of-year, daily air temperature extremes, and the previous day’s value of each; an optional variant appended the previous day’s water temperature. The accompanying Readme.txt specifies a three-stage procedure — parameter iteration, evaluation of the resulting parameter set, and reconstruction of the selected model — which this project retained.

Two design elements from this source persist in the current model: day-of-year as an explicit seasonal predictor, and the antecedent water temperature at the site as a feature. mfjd-ann-in-R.R reproduces the original workflow in R (neuralnet, caret) against the same inputs, to confirm transfer of the method prior to changing basins.

2. Model class selection

The method was applied to RM 8.5 in rm85-ann.Rmd, substituting Camp Polk discharge and temperature, NWS air temperature and cloud cover, and RM 8.5 daily maximum temperature as the response. A random forest was fitted to the identical feature matrix for comparison.

The two model classes performed comparably, with the ANN marginally ahead. Numeric results from that comparison are not reported here: the evaluation design was subsequently found to be invalid (Section 3), and the figures it produced are not interpretable as forecast skill. The comparison is recorded as a qualitative finding only — the classes were close enough that the choice between them was not determined by accuracy.

Random forests were adopted on that basis. The considerations were practical: the RF requires no predictor scaling, no architecture search and no convergence management; it yields permutation-based variable importances that support interpretation of model behaviour, which matters for a model informing regulatory decisions; and it is simpler to retrain and deploy operationally. The ANN was not developed further.

This decision has not been revisited under the current design (Section 9). It rests on a comparison whose numbers are no longer trusted, and should be regarded as provisional.

3. Feature construction and validation design

3.1 Exploratory grid and its exclusion

rm85-rf.Rmd evaluated two response variables (daily Tmax; 7DADM) against three lag structures and three lead times. No performance figures from this grid, or from the ANN comparison in Section 2, are reported in this document. Three independent defects in the evaluation design mean the reported metrics do not measure forecast skill. They are set out below because each one determined a corresponding element of the current design, which is the durable output of that phase.

One substantive finding survives and was retained: 7DADM was adopted as the response variable, being the quantity to which the HCP threshold applies.

3.2 Lag predictors postdating forecast issuance

In build_df(), all inputs are joined on the target date; the lagged specifications then select the preceding row, yielding a predictor evaluated at target_date − 1. For a forecast issued on run date R at lead k, the target date is R + k, so the lag resolves to:

lag date=R+k−1\text{lag date} = R + k - 1

This coincides with the issue date only at k = 1. At k = 3 the predictor postdates forecast issuance by two days, and at k = 7 by six days. The affected predictors include the antecedent water temperature at the response site — that is, an observation of the response variable itself, one day prior to the date being predicted.

Consequence for the design: all predictors are now constructed relative to the issue date (Section 3.5).

3.3 Two further sources of optimistic bias

Two additional issues affect the exploratory results, including the specifications carrying no lag predictors at all.

Lead-invariant weather inputs. The archive supplying the forecast predictors (all_historical_forecasts) stores a single value per issue date, replicated across all seven lead times, and therefore carries no lead-specific information. In specifications without lag predictors this is the only lead-dependent input, so those specifications were in effect fitting the same information at every lead — which is consistent with the near-constant error across lead times observed throughout the grid. This property is demonstrated in vignette("air-temperature-source").

Consequence for the design: the weather source was replaced (Section 5).

Random partitioning of an autocorrelated series. Both exploratory documents partitioned observations at random (caret::createDataPartition; sample()). Daily water temperature at this site is strongly autocorrelated:

d7 <- rm_8_5_historical |>
  filter(statistic == "7DADM", !is.na(temperature)) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) |>
  arrange(date)

consecutive <- d7 |>
  mutate(prev = lag(temperature), gap = as.numeric(date - lag(date))) |>
  filter(gap == 1, !is.na(prev))

c(n_pairs = nrow(consecutive),
  lag1_correlation = round(cor(consecutive$temperature, consecutive$prev), 4),
  mean_abs_daily_change_C = round(mean(abs(consecutive$temperature - consecutive$prev)), 3))
#>                 n_pairs        lag1_correlation mean_abs_daily_change_C 
#>               2835.0000                  0.9958                  0.3150

At a lag-1 correlation of 0.996 and a mean absolute daily change of 0.31 °C against a seasonal range of approximately 15 °C, random partitioning places the immediate temporal neighbours of most held-out observations in the training set. The effect is amplified for 7DADM, a seven-day rolling mean, for which consecutive values share six of seven constituent observations by construction.

Consequence for the design: subsequent work partitions chronologically, holding out the most recent 20% of observations.

3.4 Effect of the three defects

The three defects are not alternative explanations for the same optimism; they act independently and at different points. Lag predictors postdating issuance (3.2) affect only the lagged specifications, and only at leads greater than one. Lead-invariant weather inputs (3.3) affect every specification, and are the sole cause of flat performance across leads where no lag predictors are present. Random partitioning (3.3) affects every specification at every lead. No combination of these can be corrected after the fact from the reported figures, which is why none are reproduced here.

3.5 Run-date-relative construction

All predictors in the current model are constructed by explicit date-shifted joins evaluated as of the forecast issue date, rather than by row-position lags applied after a target-date join. Forecast trajectory predictors air_max_d1 … air_max_dk are truncated at each model’s own lead time, since day k coincides with the target date and later days describe conditions after it.

4. Evaluation framework

Model selection is based on a hindcast over the 2026 season (analysis/summer_2026_8_5_performance.Rmd), in which saved models are re-run against observations from a real RM 8.5 logger using the NWS forecasts logged operationally each day (output/nws-forecasts-log.csv). This evaluation is used in preference to historical hold-out performance because it is the only one in which the weather predictors take the form encountered in operation.

The distinction is material. The models are trained on an archived weather series but served real NWS forecasts, and the two disagree by 1.7 °C MAE at lead 1, increasing to 2.8 °C at lead 7 (cloud cover: +15 percentage points, correlation declining to 0.58). Historical hold-out evaluation uses the archived series on both sides of the comparison and cannot detect the resulting degradation.

Two reporting practices were adopted following this work. Bias is reported alongside RMSE, a systematic error of 0.6–0.8 °C having previously been present in historical test results but not reported. Skill is reported against persistence — carrying the issue-date observation forward — as a minimum standard for a forecast to be considered useful.

6. Rationale for the change-from-today formulation

6.1 Problem

Under the absolute-temperature response, hindcast performance exhibited a negative bias increasing with lead time and concentrated above the regulatory threshold: −0.90 °C at lead 1 to −1.91 °C at lead 7, and −1.03 °C mean bias on days observed at or above 20 °C. At lead 7 the model did not meaningfully improve on persistence (RMSE 2.01 versus 2.05).

6.2 Candidate explanations tested

Extrapolation beyond the training range was evaluated and rejected as the mechanism. Training data contained 31% of observations at or above 20 °C, with a maximum (24.06 °C) exceeding the 2026 maximum (23.12 °C), and the gap between maximum predicted and maximum observed values did not exceed 0.9 °C.

Two structural explanations were supported. First, the train/serve mismatch in the weather predictors described in Section 4. Second, a shift in the relationship between Camp Polk and RM 8.5 temperature occurring around 2022: a relationship estimated on 2011–2015 underpredicts 2022, 2024 and 2025 by approximately 1.9–2.1 °C, and the residual is level rather than trending, indicating a persistent regime change rather than gradual drift.

6.3 Formulation

The model is fitted to the difference between the response and the site observation available at forecast issue:

Δk=7DADM(R+k)−7DADM(R)\Delta_k = \text{7DADM}(R + k) - \text{7DADM}(R)

with the prediction reconstructed as 7DADM̂(R+k)=7DADM(R)+Δ̂k\widehat{\text{7DADM}}(R+k) = \text{7DADM}(R) + \widehat{\Delta}_k. The issue-date observation is retained in the predictor set, allowing the magnitude of the predicted change to be conditioned on current state.

6.4 Stationarity of the response variable

The formulation’s principal justification is that Δk\Delta_k is approximately stationary across years whereas the level is not. This can be evaluated directly from the historical record, independently of any model. The following summarises, by season, the mean 7DADM level and the dispersion of the seven-day change:

season <- rm_8_5_historical |>
  filter(statistic == "7DADM", !is.na(temperature)) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  filter(lubridate::month(date) %in% 5:10) |>
  mutate(delta7 = if_else(as.numeric(date - lag(date, 7)) == 7,
                          temperature - lag(temperature, 7), NA_real_))

by_year <- season |>
  group_by(year = lubridate::year(date)) |>
  summarise(level_mean = mean(temperature),
            delta_mean = mean(delta7, na.rm = TRUE),
            delta_sd   = sd(delta7,   na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(delta_sd))

summarise(by_year,
          level_mean_min = min(level_mean), level_mean_max = max(level_mean),
          delta_sd_min   = min(delta_sd),   delta_sd_max   = max(delta_sd)) |>
  round(2)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   level_mean_min level_mean_max delta_sd_min delta_sd_max
#>            <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1           13.8           18.3         1.41         2.23

Across the historical seasons the mean level varies by roughly 4.5 °C between years, while the dispersion of the seven-day change occupies a narrow band and its mean sits near zero in every season. The quantity the absolute formulation must predict therefore relocates substantially from year to year; the quantity the change formulation must predict does not.

The 2026 season provides an out-of-sample test of this property. Its mean level, 21.3 °C, lies above every season in the historical record and approximately 4.6 °C above the historical mean of seasonal means. Its seven-day change has a standard deviation of 1.89 °C, which falls inside the historical range, and a 5th–95th percentile span of −2.1 to +3.9 °C against a historical span of −3.2 to +2.8 °C. The level moved outside all prior experience; the change did not.

6.5 Rationale

Three distinct mechanisms follow from Section 6.4, addressing the error sources identified in Section 6.2.

(i) Location of exposure to predictor error. Under an absolute response the model must reconstruct the temperature level from its predictors, and the weather predictors — those subject to the train/serve mismatch of Section 4 — participate directly in that reconstruction. Error in them propagates into the level, increasingly with lead time as forecast quality declines. Under the change formulation the level is supplied by 7DADM(R)\text{7DADM}(R), a direct observation of the response variable at the site, identical in training and in operation and not subject to the mismatch. Predictor error can corrupt the estimated change but not the level to which that change is applied.

(ii) Relaxation of the range constraint. A random forest returns an average of response values held in its terminal nodes and therefore cannot predict outside the range represented in training. Twenty percent of 2026 observations exceeded the training maximum, so under an absolute response those values were not attainable. Under the change formulation the level enters additively and outside the model, so a prediction may exceed the training range provided the estimated change lies within it — and by Section 6.4 it generally does.

The failure of the seasonal anomaly predictors (Table 1) supports this reading. Those predictors were introduced on the expectation of improving performance in an anomalous season and degraded it significantly. In 2026, 61% of anomaly values exceeded the training 95th percentile and 13% exceeded the training maximum, leaving the predictor saturated for much of the season while continuing to occupy candidate-split positions. Supplying the anomaly as a predictor reintroduces precisely the range constraint that the change formulation removes by handling the level outside the model.

(iii) Allocation of model capacity. A substantial share of the variance in the absolute response is seasonal climatology. Under an absolute response the model expends capacity re-deriving the annual cycle from day-of-year and related predictors. Supplying the level directs the whole model to the departure from it, which is the component that is genuinely uncertain and that the predictors are informative about.

6.6 Interpretation of fit statistics

Δk\Delta_k has substantially smaller variance than the level. A model fitted to it may therefore report a lower R² on its own response while producing more accurate temperature forecasts, since R² is scaled by the variance of the quantity being predicted. Comparisons between the two formulations are made on bias and RMSE of the reconstructed temperature, which is the quantity of operational interest and is on a common scale across formulations.

6.7 Verification against persistence

Because the formulation is anchored on persistence, it was verified that it does not reduce to it. On the 2026 hindcast the model outperforms persistence at every lead time, with the margin increasing from 0.18 °C at lead 1 to 0.76 °C at lead 7. A model coasting on the anchor would show the opposite pattern, the margin narrowing as the anchor became less informative. The effect size of the formulation change (Table 1) is six to ten times that of the weather source substitution, which was not significant.

6.8 Conditions and limitations

The formulation depends on conditions that hold at this site but are not general.

An observation of the response must be available at forecast issue. The approach was not available earlier in this project: prior to installation of the RM 8.5 logger, the corresponding predictor was a stand-in drawn from the historical record, and anchoring on a substituted value would not have conferred the properties described above.

The response must be autocorrelated. The anchor is informative only because 7DADM is strongly persistent (Section 3.3). The approach would not transfer to a weakly autocorrelated response.

The anchor becomes a single point of failure. Error in 7DADM(R)\text{7DADM}(R) propagates directly and undiminished into every forecast. Sensor reliability is correspondingly more consequential under this formulation than under an absolute one.

The anchor’s value decays with lead time. At seven days it remains clearly beneficial (Section 6.7). At longer horizons persistence weakens and a blend toward climatology would be expected to outperform a persistence anchor; the point at which this occurs has not been established.

6.9 Relation to established methods

The formulation is an instance of a general approach rather than a novel one, and appears under several names: differencing in time-series analysis, where it is applied for the same reason — to render a non-stationary series stationary before modelling; anomaly or increment forecasting in numerical weather prediction post-processing; and residual learning in machine learning, where a model is fitted to H(x)−xH(x) - x rather than H(x)H(x). Gradient boosting is a sequential application of the same principle. The operative heuristic is that where a current observation of an autocorrelated response is available, the change is generally the better modelling target.

7. Current model specification

Separate random forests (500 trees, mtry = ⌊p/3⌋) for lead times 1–7, fitted to Δk\Delta_k on the May–October season, 2021–2025, with a chronological 80/20 partition. Predictors: Camp Polk discharge, 7DADM and daily maximum with five-day trends; dynamical.org GFS forecast trajectory (daily maximum and minimum air temperature, cloud cover, day-of-year for each day d1 … dk); trajectory summaries; and RM 8.5 issue-date 7DADM, daily maximum, and five-day trends. Implemented in analysis/rm85-rf-delta.Rmd; saved as output/rm85_rf_7dadm_delta_lead{1..7}.rds.

Site observations are taken from the issue date rather than the preceding day. The operational job runs at 19:00 PST and the site’s daily maximum occurs by 17:00–18:00 on effectively all observed days (0% after 19:00; 4.1% after 18:00), so the issue-date value is complete at run time.

A quantile regression forest is fitted alongside on the same response and predictors (analysis/rm85-rf-delta-quantiles.Rmd), supplying prediction intervals and exceedance probability. Nominal intervals were found to over-cover; calibrated levels are stored in output/rm85_qrf_interval_calibration.csv.

8. Performance

Table 2. 2026 hindcast performance, current formulation (n = 83 per lead).

Lead (days) Bias (°C) MAE (°C) RMSE (°C) Persistence RMSE (°C)
1 −0.05 0.21 0.27 0.45
2 −0.01 0.32 0.41 0.81
3 −0.01 0.44 0.54 1.09
4 −0.02 0.58 0.74 1.33
5 −0.07 0.70 0.88 1.53
6 −0.07 0.79 1.01 1.68
7 −0.19 0.81 1.01 1.77

Bias on days observed at or above the threshold ranges from −0.05 °C at lead 1 to −0.45 °C at lead 7, against −0.63 to −1.76 °C under the previous formulation.

Threshold-exceedance sensitivity ranges from 0.91 to 0.96 across lead times. Missed exceedances occur on six dates, clustered around the three occasions in the season on which the observed series first crossed the threshold from below; the remaining dates are trailing days of the same events. Missed cases are marginal rather than large errors: 85% were observed below 20.5 °C, with a median forecast 0.6 °C below threshold and a median required rise of 1.8 °C against a median of approximately 0 °C across all forecast dates.

9. Status, limitations and open questions

The current formulation is a working specification, not a settled result. The following are unresolved.

Validation is limited to a single, anomalous season. The 2026 hindcast covers 83 forecast dates in the warmest year of the record. Performance in a season of typical warmth has not been observed, and the interval calibration in particular should be re-derived once it has been.

The model has not been retrained on 2026 observations. Twenty percent of 2026 observations exceeded the training maximum. Incorporating the season would extend the covered range and is expected to be the single largest available improvement.

Uncertainty in the weather predictors is not represented. The quantile model characterises the conditional distribution of water temperature given the supplied forecast; it does not represent error in that forecast, which is the dominant error source at lead 7. Propagation through a GEFS ensemble would address this.

Interval coverage is calibrated empirically rather than guaranteed. Conformalized quantile regression would provide finite-sample coverage guarantees while retaining lead-dependent adaptivity.

The operational forecast log is the preferred long-term training source. Once output/nws-forecasts-log.csv spans two to three seasons, the distribution of realised forecast errors will incorporate model error, weather-input error and regime drift jointly, and is expected to supersede archive-based uncertainty estimation.

Model class selection rests on a discarded evaluation. The ANN/RF comparison in Section 2 was made under the design later found invalid, and its figures are not reported for that reason. The choice of random forest therefore rests on the practical considerations set out in Section 2 — interpretability, absence of tuning, operational simplicity — rather than on a measured accuracy comparison. It also predates the change-from-today formulation, run-date-relative feature construction, and the current weather source. Gradient boosting was superior under the absolute response and inferior after the weather source changed; neither result has been re-tested under the current specification. Re-running the class comparison under the current design and a chronological partition is the cleanest way to put this on a measured footing.

Regime stability is assumed and not monitored. The Camp Polk to RM 8.5 relationship shifted once within the record. No automated check on trailing forecast bias is currently in place.
